This historical performance demonstrates an underlying operational capacity that is not reflected in the current market capitalization of ₹ 16.1 Cr [E2]. Conceded: the current ROE of -25.2% [E12], the ROCE of -24.8% [E11], and the ROA of -552.34% [E7] indicate significant recent headwinds. However, the stock is trading at only 33% of its 52-week range [E4], suggesting that the market has aggressively discounted the equity despite the company's demonstrated long-term potential for high returns [E19]. By focusing exclusively on the recent negative ROE [E55], the market ignores the structural evidence of the company's historical profitability [E46].

Furthermore, the company offers no dividend yield to compensate shareholders for these risks [E3]. While the company has demonstrated a 3-year median return on equity of 43% [E19], conceded: [E46], this historical metric is overshadowed by the current reality of a -25.2% return on equity [E12]. The recent collapse in profitability, marked by a -25% median return on equity over the last year [E20], confirms that the business is currently failing to generate value for its owners [E55].

The bear’s focus on current ROE [E12, E20] ignores the company’s proven capacity for high-level performance, as evidenced by a 3-year median ROE of 43% [E19, E46]. Conceded: the current ROE is -25.2% [E12] and the ROCE is -24.8% [E11]. The bear’s critique of the 6.19x price-to-book ratio [E1] lacks context, as it ignores that the company is currently trading at only 33% of its 52-week high [E4], suggesting the market has already heavily discounted the recent volatility. By fixating solely on the most recent annual figures [E55], the bear overlooks the established track record of profitability that justifies a premium over a distressed sector [E46]. The absence of a dividend [E3] is a common feature of companies currently reinvesting or restructuring to return to their historical 43% ROE levels [E19].

The bull claims the 6.19x price-to-book ratio [E1] is justified by the stock trading at 33% of its 52-week range [E4], but this ignores that investors are paying a premium for a company currently destroying capital rather than generating it [E11, E12].
